title: Broker kills the connection while a warm shutdown drains running tasks
title_original: Fix: Broker heartbeats not sent during graceful shutdown
text_original:
## Description

Full disclosure: I used Claude Code to help me understand the code base and propose fixes. I made sure to understand the architecture as well as I could, and carefully reviewed all code changes myself and tested them successfully on a system with a production workload for several days.

The root cause of broker heartbeats not being sent during graceful shutdown is that the event loop (`asynloop()` in `celery/worker/loops.py`) exits before the prefork `TaskPool` can drain tasks that are still in progress. The lack of an event loop causes timers not to fire, which are responsible for sending heartbeats on the broker connection. These heartbeats are registered with the timer component by the `_enable_amqheartbeats()` function in `loops.py`.

As I understand things, the following architectural dependencies exist during runtime and graceful shutdown:

- The Timer component relies on the Hub event loop firing
- The Hub component relies on the Consumer event loop to fire timers (asynloop)
- The Pool component relies on the Consumer in order to consume and acknowledge tasks
- The Consumer must stop first, in order to stop new tasks from being consumed

I tried to come up with various fixes that were straightforward and did not violate areas of concern between components, but each component is tied to another, causing a dependency chain that cannot be easily changed.

I believe that the fixes in this pull request address the problem while making as few changes as possible to the code. The high-level description is that the Pool component temporarily starts a new thread during shutdown that will keep firing the hub event loop (and therefore timers). Once the pool is finished draining, the thread is stopped. This successfully keeps the broker connection alive so that tasks that eventually drain can still acknowledge the broker messages.

I removed two different locations where timers were prematurely shut down or cleared (one of these via `hub.reset()`). Clearing timers in the event loop or Consumer component appears to violate areas of responsibility. I would expect that only the Timer component should be responsible for cleaning up timers.

My understanding is that these timer cleanup changes are safe to make because the Pool component needs the timers to continue existing, and the eventual shutdown of the timer component itself will still clean up timers properly. I also added a line of code to the Hub component initialization to ensure that the kombu poller object is initialized, now that the asynloop function no longer resets the hub component.

I have added unit tests to cover the new code to ensure that it behaves as expected.

The fix works in my environment, because I observe that RabbitMQ no longer shows any message re-deliveries when a Celery worker is gracefully shut down and task drain time exceeds the broker heartbeat interval. I can also observe Celery worker logs that show task completion after the warm shutdown log.

As far as I understand, other pool types that use synloop do not suffer from this same problem and the fix is only required for prefork.

This is my first time contributing to Celery, so I'm happy to address any feedback in order to contribute this fix to a long-standing issue. Thank you for considering my changes and description.

Fixes #5998
text_rewritten: When a worker gets a warm-shutdown signal while long tasks are still running, the broker closes the connection long before those tasks finish, and everything that was in flight comes back as a connection error instead of a result. The connection dies because the worker stops servicing its periodic timers -- the broker heartbeat among them -- the moment its consumer loop leaves; nothing keeps the heartbeat going for the minutes the pool spends draining. Leaving the loop must stop new work from being consumed without throwing away the periodic callbacks that keep the connection alive. The one case that must still throw them away is an abnormal exit: if the loop bails out because the connection itself broke, everything it registered against the event hub is stale and has to be handed back before the error propagates.

acceptance_hint: A consumer loop that exits normally leaves the event hub untouched; a loop that exits because of a connection error resets the hub before re-raising.
